item.title: [fansided.com] Evaluating the Hall of Fame trajectories of Shohei Ohtani and MLB’s postseason stars
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

item.title: [MLB.com] Alonso y Arenado, Jugadores de la Semana; Acuña Jr. realizó la mejor jugada
item.dc:creator: Linus Lawrence
item.description: Nunca es demasiado tarde para llamar la atención. Un trío de perennes convocados al Juego de Estrellas demostró ese punto durante la última semana de la temporada regular del 2026. Pete Alonso y Nolan Arenado se destacaron en ofensiva, terminando con notas altas para ganar los últimos premios a Jugador de la Semana del año, mientras que el venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr. recibió los honores de Jugada de la Semana por su espectacular atrapada en la pista de advertencia el sábado contra los Marlins. N
item.content:encoded:
Nunca es demasiado tarde para llamar la atención. Un trío de perennes convocados al Juego de Estrellas demostró ese punto durante la última semana de la temporada regular del 2026. Pete Alonso y Nolan Arenado se destacaron en ofensiva, terminando con notas altas para ganar los últimos premios a Jugador de la Semana del año, mientras que el venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr. recibió los honores de Jugada de la Semana por su espectacular atrapada en la pista de advertencia el sábado contra los Marlins.
Nueva York parece despertar algo dentro del Oso Polar. Después de conectar el jonrón número 300 de su carrera en el Citi Field el 15 de septiembre, Alonso necesitó de apenas ocho partidos más para alcanzar el número 307 – un impresionante batazo de 471 pies – en una actuación de dos cuadrangulares en el Yankee Stadium el viernes por la noche. En sus últimos cinco compromisos en Toronto y en el Bronx, Alonso se embasó en 11 de sus 22 visitas al plato, registrando cinco vuelacercas, ocho carreras impulsadas y ocho anotadas. El esfuerzo le valió al primera base su segundo premio a Jugador de la Semana de la segunda mitad de la campaña.
A pesar de que el último juego de la temporada de los Orioles fue cancelado debido al tiempo, Alonso superó al cubano Yordan Álvarez para encabezar la Liga Americana en cuadrangulares (43) y empujadas (113). Anteriormente, lideró la Liga Nacional en remolcadas con los Mets en el 2022 (131), convirtiéndose en el primer jugador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas en liderar ambas ligas en impulsadas. También jugó en todos los partidos de su equipo por tercera campaña consecutiva.
Los D-backs no pudieron completar su intento por conseguir el tercer Comodín de la Liga Nacional, pero su antesalista veterano hizo casi todo lo posible para llevarlos hasta allí. Después de conectar un grand slam decisivo contra los Yankees el 20 de septiembre, Arenado terminó a un triple del ciclo en el Coors Field el martes. En los últimos seis encuentros de las Serpientes en Colorado y San Diego, Arenado tuvo 10 hits en 23 turnos al bate (.435) con tres cuadrangulares, dos dobles y cinco empujadas.
Con un jonrón de dos carreras en San Diego el viernes, el jugador de 35 años registró su octava temporada de 30 cuadrangulares o más y su primera desde el 2022 con los Cardenales. Los únicos jugadores con más campañas de 30 vuelacercas como antesalistas titulares son los miembros del Salón de la Fama Mike Schmidt (12) y Eddie Mathews (10).
Acuña tiene una historia complicada con los jardines del loanDepot park. En marzo de este año, ganó un campeonato del Clásico Mundial de Béisbol allí con la selección de Venezuela, pero en julio del 2021, el jardinero derecho se rompió el ligamento cruzado anterior derecho mientras saltaba cerca de la cerca, dejándolo fuera del resto de la campaña en que los Bravos ganaron la Serie Mundial. El sábado por la tarde, menos de 72 horas antes de comenzar una carrera por otro título, Acuña demostró que realmente no le tiene miedo de la pista de advertencia de Miami.
Sin outs y con un corredor en primera en el primer inning, el toletero dominicano de los Marlins, Heriberto Hernández, elevó un sinker de Brent Suter por la banda contraria a 101.2 millas por hora. Acuña corrió a su derecha a 25.6 pies por segundo, saltó hacia la cerca y cayó al suelo con la pelota asegurada, dándoles a los Bravos un ruidoso primer out del juego. (Hernández continuó y registró su 25º jonrón al día siguiente, sabiamente llevando la pelota al jardín izquierdo en lugar de poner a prueba a Acuña nuevamente.)

item.title: [MLB.com] Alonso, Arenado earn Player of the Week honors with epic finishes

item.description: It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins. item.content:encoded:
It’s never too late to make a statement. A trio of perennial All-Stars proved that point during the final week of the 2026 regular season. Pete Alonso and Nolan Arenado went on offensive tears, finishing on resounding high notes to earn the year’s last Player of the Week Awards, while Ronald Acuña Jr. received Play of the Week honors for his spectacular warning-track grab on Saturday against the Marlins.
New York seems to awaken something within the Polar Bear. After hitting his 300th career homer back at Citi Field on Sept. 15, Alonso needed just eight more games to notch No. 307 – a jaw-dropping 471 foot shot – in a two-homer performance at Yankee Stadium on Friday night. Over his last five games in Toronto and the Bronx, Alonso reached base in 11 of his 22 plate appearances, recording five homers, eight RBIs and eight runs scored. The effort earned the first baseman his second Player of the Week Award of the second half.
Even with the Orioles’ final game of the season cancelled due to inclement weather, Alonso outpaced Yordan Alvarez to lead the American League in homers (43) and RBIs (113). He previously led the National League in RBIs with the Mets in 2022 (131), making him the first player in Major League history to lead both leagues in RBIs. He also played in every one of his team’s games for a third consecutive season.
The D-backs couldn’t complete their bid for the third NL Wild Card spot, but their veteran third baseman did just about everything he could to will them there. A game after hitting a go-ahead grand slam against the Yankees on Sept. 21, he finished a triple shy of the cycle at Coors Field on Tuesday to commence the ninth Player of the Week campaign of his career. Over the Snakes’ final six games in Colorado and San Diego, Arenado went 10-for-23 (.435) with three homers, two doubles and 5 RBIs.
With a two-run home run in San Diego on Friday, the 35-year-old notched his eighth 30-homer season and his first since 2022 with the Cardinals. The only players with more 30-homer seasons as primary third basemen are Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12) and Eddie Mathews (10).
Acuña has a complicated history with the loanDepot park outfield. This March, he clinched a World Baseball Classic championship there with Team Venezuela; but in July 2021, the right fielder tore his right ACL while leaping for a ball near the fence, sidelining him for the remainder of the Braves’ World Series campaign. On Saturday afternoon, less than 72 hours before kicking off a run at another title, Acuña proved he truly has no fear of the Miami warning track.
With no outs and a runner on first in the opening frame, Marlins slugger Heriberto Hernández lofted a Brent Suter sinker the opposite way at 101.2 mph. Acuña darted to his right at 25.6 feet per second, leapt at the fence and went tumbling to the dirt with the ball secured, giving the Braves a loud first out of the game. (Hernández went on to record his 25th homer the next day, wisely pulling the ball to left field rather than testing Acuña again.)

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] MLB wild-card preview: Series predictions, X-factors and more for Red Sox-Yankees, Cubs-Padres, Phillies-Braves and White Sox-Astros
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical. Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins. AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves Projected starters (all times ET) Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luza
item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [FanSided] Ronald Acuña Jr. quietly just gave baseball another reason to fear the Braves
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: At some point, you’ve probably heard the one about the guy who walks into a doctor’s office, or the horse who walks into a bar. In the case of Atlanta Braves superstar outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr., his story involves the man who walks into the batter’s box, subtly changes his stance and catches fire ahead of the playoffs. item.content:encoded:
At some point, you’ve probably heard the one about the guy who walks into a doctor’s office, or the horse who walks into a bar. In the case of Atlanta Braves superstar outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr., his story involves the man who walks into the batter’s box, subtly changes his stance and catches fire ahead of the playoffs.
As Major League Baseball’s Mark Bowman recently pointed out, the 2023 NL MVP made a slight tweak to his hitting approach late last month. Mired in a prolonged slump following two hamstring strains, Acuña Jr. did not play in an Aug. 27 win over the eventual NL West champion Dodgers.
Later that night, Acuña Jr. told Braves assistant coach Eddie Pérez he wanted to take early batting practice the next day. During said session, the five-time All-Star closed his stance and, according to Bowman, "backed off the plate a couple of inches [and] separated his feet another few inches.”
The results? Let’s just say the rest of Major League Baseball should be on high alert.
How Atlanta Braves superstar Ronald Acuña Jr. changed his stance and turned his season around
Entering play Sunday, Acuña Jr. is hitting .337 with seven home runs, 20 RBI and a .997 OPS in 112 plate appearances since returning to the lineup on Aug. 28. His batting average has skyrocketed from .235 to .255, and his OPS went from .748 to .796 in less than a month.
If you extrapolate those stats over a full season, Acuña Jr. would finish with 44 home runs, 37 doubles and 125 RBI. Here’s where things get especially interesting: Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez is considered the consensus AL MVP favorite, and he woke up Sunday hitting .316 with 42 home runs, 105 RBI and a 1.036 OPS.
But wait, you say. Acuña Jr. plays in the National League, so how would those numbers compare to Cubs star outfielder and MVP shoo-in Pete Crow-Armstrong? Great question. Crow-Armstrong entered Sunday hitting .278 with 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 31 doubles, 41 steals and a .941 OPS. In that case, we’re not sure whether PCA would be running away with the NL MVP.
“When he is healthy and he gets on one of these streaks, he’s one of the best players in baseball,” said Ozzie Albies, who has played with Acuña since the latter’s 2018 debut. “There's nothing else to say about that.”
Arguably the most remarkable part is how Acuña Jr. responded to sitting during a playoff race. Keep in mind the Braves only had a five-game NL East lead over the Phillies when the veteran outfielder rejoined the lineup on Aug. 28. But rather than complain or take things personally, Acuña Jr. took it upon himself to fix what wasn’t working.
Fans and observers can say whatever they want about Acuña Jr., who has frequently drawn pushback for his enthusiasm, celebrations and durability. But he was injured during the Braves’ 2021 title run, and he’s still chasing his first World Series plate appearance. He turns 29 in December and only has two years of team control left; time is running out for him to guarantee himself a nine-figure contract.
But if Acuña Jr. continues to hit how he has of late, the only question is whether he’ll clear $250 million on his next deal. Guiding the Braves to their second championship in six years would go a long way in convincing ownership he’s still worth the risk.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Why Ben Rice's MVP case deserves more love in a lost Aaron Judge season
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Without Aaron Judge for most of the season, the AL MVP race is wide open. The favorite for much of the year has been Houston Astros slugger Yordan Álvarez, but he's far from a sure thing. The New York Yankees have seen Cam Schlittler's candidacy get more recognition in recent weeks, but there's another Yankee who's being grossly overlooked. item.content:encoded:
Without Aaron Judge for most of the season, the AL MVP race is wide open. The favorite for much of the year has been Houston Astros slugger Yordan Álvarez, but he's far from a sure thing. The New York Yankees have seen Cam Schlittler's candidacy get more recognition in recent weeks, but there's another Yankee who's being grossly overlooked.
Ben Rice was obviously a breakout star for New York last season, but this year he has reached a new gear. Aaron Boone predicted that Rice would clock 39 dingers this season, which was the total the Dartmouth product was sitting on when the Yankees took on the Tampa Bay Rays on September 23, with five games left to play. Neither team had anything left to play for with playoff positions solidified, so it seemed like a good chance that Rice would finish at that number.
But just like that, the 27-year-old bested his manager when he led off the bottom of the first with a solo shot. That wasn't all, though, as Rice came back up to the plate to lead off the bottom of the fourth and smacked his second tater of the game. He now sits at 41 homers and enters the Yankees' record book as a result.
His 40th blast of the year put him in some elite company in franchise history. Rice became just the eighth Yankee to hit 40 or more homers in a season at age 27 or younger. The rest of the list includes four inner-circle Hall of Famers: Babe Ruth (twice), Lou Gehrig (twice), Mickey Mantle (twice), and Joe DiMaggio. In addition to those four, the other three are former single-season home run king Roger Maris, Juan Soto, and, of course, Judge.
Ben Rice's 40th homer underscores how incredibly valuable he's been to the Yankees in Aaron Judge's absence
MLB.com's latest awards poll has Rice as a distant fifth in the voting, behind Álvarez, Junior Caminero, Bobby Witt Jr., and Schlittler, in that order. There are a few things that don't make much sense here.
Álvarez has been great this year, but there's a narrative among some that he's been Judge-like that just isn't true. Air Yordan has posted a 181 wRC+ through September 23, which is still over 20 points lower than Judge's 203 mark last season, which also happened to be the lowest wRC+ he has put up in any of his three MVP campaigns. That's relevant because he is seeking to become the first full-time DH to take home the honor other than Shohei Ohtani.
As for Caminero, he began generating a lot of MVP buzz with his two walk-off homers in mid-September, as if those wins somehow count more than victories at any other point during the season. More importantly, Rice has caught up to him, as both now have 41 homers. Rice has also surpassed him in on-base percentage (.362 versus .360) and slugging percentage (.537 versus .523).
The DH argument also works against Rice, but only to an extent. He's played 55 games at first base and has mostly ceded playing time in the field to accommodate trade deadline acquisition Luis Garcia Jr. It should also be noted that Caminero isn't a great defensive third baseman and is last among qualifiers at the position with -11 outs above average.
More importantly, there's the Judge factor in all of this. The Astros are on the brink of either missing the playoffs for the second year in a row or winning the most pathetic division in MLB history, dipping under .500 late in the campaign. The Rays have had their big boppers like Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda healthy for most of the year.
Losing a player as singular as Judge is a huge blow to a team, but the Yankees are playoff-bound yet again. Throw in a lengthy absence from Cody Bellinger and the fact that they're starting to print milk cartons with Giancarlo Stanton's face on them, and it's been Rice who has kept the offense afloat all year.
If the point of this exercise is to recognize the player who has been the most valuable, then the loss of Judge looms large. We've had our frustrations, but the Yankees really haven't skipped a beat without Judge and his enormous value. Rice is a big reason why, and while it might not be enough to win him the award, he should be a much larger part of the conversation.

item.title: [Pittsburgh Baseball Now] Pirates’ Nick Gonzales Positioned to End Year in Exclusive Group of .300 Hitters

item.content:encoded:
Pirates’ Nick Gonzales Positioned to End Year in Exclusive Group of .300 Hitters
Only seven players enter the final day of the 2026 season with a batting average of .300 or better. Pirates infielder Nick Gonzales (.302) is one of them.
Gonzales has a chance to be the first qualified hitter for the Pirates to finish with a batting average of .300 or better since teammate Bryan Reynolds hit .302 in 2021.
While accomplishing the feat would be “cool,” Gonzales is not stepping into the batter’s box thinking about his batting average.
“You just try to be consistent every single day and if that’s where I am, that’s where I am,” he explained. “It’s something that could really eat you up if you really focus on it too much throughout the year. I just play my game and try to be consistent.”
Batting average is considered to be an antiquated stat by some in today’s game. Given Gonzales’ profile and background, he’s someone who sees the value in hitting for average.
“I think it’s still a testament to finding ways to get hits,” he said. “I’m not a guy who’s gonna just swing for home runs. That’s not really my game. So, you gotta kinda learn how to find hits.”
The six other qualified hitters who join Gonzales in the .300 club are the Astros’ Yordan Alvarez (.316), Diamondbacks’ Gabriel Moreno (.311), Phillies’ Luis Arraez (.310), Rays Chandler Simpson (.306), Marlins’ Otto Lopez (.305) and Rockies’ TJ Rumfield (.300).
10 years ago, 25 hitters finished with a .300 batting average. The fact now that so few hitters are able to finish at or above the mark is a testament to the quality of pitchers in today’s game, Gonzales believes.
“I don’t think hitters are worse,” he said. “I think it’s just that the pitching is that good.”
Gonzales’ offensive showing with the Pirates this season has been the best of his career. But while his offense has been a bright spot this season, his defense has lagged well behind.
Gonzales, a natural second baseman, has been tasked with manning a new position. After adding Brandon Lowe at second base in the offseason, the Pirates had to shift Gonzales to third base. The 27-year-old has committed 11 errors in 112 games at the hot corner with minus-15 defensive runs saved.
While Gonzales hasn’t had the year he’s wanted defensively, he’s not allowed his fielding woes to carry over to the plate.
“You don’t take your glove to hit and you don’t take your bat to play defense. So, just flush it. Forget about it,” he explained. “As soon as I step back in the box, it’s over with.”
Through all of the defensive inconsistencies this season, Gonzales has remained a steady presence in the Pirates’ lineup. Finishing the season in what will be an exclusive group of players with a .300 batting average would be a reflection of the progress he’s made offensively this season.
“He should take pride in that, in how he’s been able to swing the bat for us,” said manager Don Kelly. “He’s had some huge at-bats and swung the bat well. He’s been a big part of our offensive success this year.”
More about:Pirates

(AP) — Yordan Alvarez launched a three-run homer and the Houston Astros went deep five times Saturday night as they moved closer to a division title with a 13-2 victory over the Athletics. item.content:encoded:
WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Yordan Alvarez launched a three-run homer and the Houston Astros went deep five times Saturday night as they moved closer to a division title with a 13-2 victory over the Athletics.
Houston (80-81) can clinch the AL West crown and the No. 3 seed in the American League playoffs with another win Sunday over the A’s in their regular-season finale or a Texas Rangers loss at Minnesota. Either team will become the first to win a division with a .500 record or worse, excluding shortened seasons.
Alvarez homered in the fifth inning to put the Astros up 6-1. His 42nd homer of the season tied him with Tampa Bay slugger Junior Caminero for second in the AL.
Houston finished with 16 hits as Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes and Jose Altuve combined for nine of them and seven RBIs.
Peña hit a pair of two-run homers, one in the third and the other in the eighth. He finished 4 for 6 with four RBIs. Parades homered in the first to open the scoring and went 3 for 5.
Hayden Wesneski (6-2) threw seven innings and struck out five while allowing six hits and two runs.
The Astros scored six runs, including Lucas Spence’s solo homer, between the seventh and ninth to expand their lead to 13-2.
Jack Perkins (3-13) pitched five innings for the Athletics. He struck out nine but gave up six runs and three homers.
Up next
Neither team had announced a starting pitcher for Sunday’s regular-season finale.
___

item.description: A majority of the focus for the New York Yankees is planning their roster and preparing to host the Boston Red Sox in next week’s wild-card series. item.content:encoded:
A majority of the focus for the New York Yankees is planning their roster and preparing to host the Boston Red Sox in next week’s wild-card series.
Another area of focus will be finishing out the regular season with their 94th win when the Yankees host the Baltimore Orioles on Sunday, weather permitting.
The start time has been moved up to 1:05 p.m.
The Yankees (93-68) were off on Saturday because a nor’easter resulted in a single-admission doubleheader on Friday. Since New York was eliminated from the American League East race on Tuesday night, its past four games have seen the team give regulars time off and rest some of its prominent relievers while seeing other defensive alignments.
On Friday, the Yankees took a 10-2 loss in the opener and earned their fifth doubleheader split of the season with a 6-3 victory before the tarp was put on the field immediately after the final pitch.
Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr. were among those who rested in the opener before starting in the second game. Anthony Volpe played third base in the first game and shortstop in the second game after playing only at second base following his return from the minor leagues on Sept. 10.
Volpe had three hits in the doubleheader, including a two-run double in the sixth inning Friday night. Volpe’s newfound versatility may be something for the Yankees to consider for their postseason roster as he’s hitting .265 (11 for 49) with nine RBIs in 14 games since returning.
“This is the most important part of the season,” Volpe said. “This is the best part of why you do it; this is why you play. It’s Yankees/Red Sox — that’s what October baseball is.”
Ben Rice had three hits in the doubleheader and enters the regular-season finale with 41 homers and 97 RBIs in a year when Aaron Judge has played 66 games and may miss the wild-card series because of a moderately strained right calf.
The Orioles (79-82) are concluding their second straight losing season after winning 275 games from 2022-2024.
Pete Alonso enters Sunday with 43 homers and 113 RBIs in his first season with the Orioles. He will win the AL RBI title and is one ahead of Yordan Alvarez and Junior Caminero for the AL home run crown.
Alonso is looking to play in his 162nd game of the season for the third consecutive year.
Eight of Alonso’s past 10 hits are homers and he has the most homers by an Oriole since Mark Trumbo mashed 47 in 2016.
“It’s impressive,” manager Craig Albernaz said. “It’s not only the at-bat quality and the pitches he’s getting, he’s not missing them. He’s squaring them up pretty good.”
If the game gets played, the Yankees will get another look at Elmer Rodriguez (0-3, 5.40 ERA). Rodriguez has made six starts this season and has 21 strikeouts and 16 walks in 26 2/3 innings.
Rodriguez last pitched in the major leagues when he struggled through 3 2/3 innings during a 10-1 road loss to the Angels on Aug. 31. He also showed increased velocity Aug. 26 in a no-decision in New York’s 9-3 win over Houston when he allowed three runs on three hits in six innings.
Shane Baz (6-15, 4.11) starts for Baltimore and likely will pitch an abbreviated outing similar to Trevor Rogers, who threw 55 pitches in four innings Friday. Baz is 2-6 with a 4.37 ERA in his past 10 starts and took a no-decision Monday against Toronto when Baltimore rallied in the eighth inning.
Baz is 0-3 with a 6.48 ERA in eight career starts against the Yankees.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers get A grade in final Post MLB Power Rankings. But who gets an F?
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
Throughout the season, the California Post power-ranked MLB’s 30 teams and checked in on intriguing awards races. Records as of Saturday morning:
1) Brewers (101-59): A+
It was another perfect regular season for the Brewers, who won 100 games for the first time in franchise history to clinch the best record in the majors. Of course, their repeated failures in recent postseasons mean the real test is still to come in October. They have one superstar in Jacob Misiorowski but will need others to emerge in this year’s playoffs.
2) Dodgers (98-62): A
It was a familiar story for the Dodgers this year. A hot start. A second-half slump. Plenty of injuries along the way. Yet, another division crown that sets them up for another deep October run. That formula has worked the past two years for the two-time defending champions. Their real grade this season will depend on whether they can complete a World Series three-peat.
3) Rays (97-63): A+
After two years of missing the playoffs, the Rays had a very Rays-esque season. Uncovered gems on the mound. A relentlessly consistent lineup at the plate. And, as a result, the AL’s best record — and their best chance to get back to the World Series since 2020.
4) Braves (93-67): A
The Braves are back in the playoffs and back atop the NL East, rebounding as hoped from a disappointing 86-loss campaign last season that snapped a six-year postseason streak.
5) Yankees (93-68): B+
This grade might’ve been higher, if not for the uncertainty shrouding the Bronx Bombers as they enter the postseason. They managed to survive one extended Aaron Judge absence this regular season. Trying to do so again in October would be a tall task.
6) Padres (89-71): A-
In the weeks leading up to the trade deadline, the Padres seemed bound to be sellers. But then their offense — especially Fernando Tatis Jr. — came back to life. They bolstered their rotation by being buyers at the trade deadline instead. And now they are back in the playoffs as a potential dark horse, thanks to their 16-5 record in September.
7) Cubs (88-73): B+
The Cubs are back in the playoffs for a second straight year. They have the presumptive National League MVP in Pete Crow-Armstrong. And they managed to overcome a wave of pitching injuries. Now, they will try to mount a deeper October run after being knocked out in Game 5 of the NLDS last year.
8) Red Sox (87-74): B+
A strange regular season in Boston has reached a satisfactory ending, with the Red Sox — led by interim-now-turned-permanent manager Chad Tracy — getting a shot to avenge last year’s postseason elimination to the Yankees in next week’s wild-card series.
9) Phillies (87-73): Incomplete
Check back with us on Sunday night for this final grade. Because after seemingly salvaging their nightmarish start to the season under interim manager Don Mattingly, the Phillies are flirting with what would be a monumental September collapse, having yet to secure their place in the playoffs amid a 2-5 slump this week.
10) Diamondbacks (86-74): B-
We are only tentatively grading the Dbacks for now, thanks to their slim (but very much possible) chances of sneaking into the playoffs. If they don’t, it will be another conflicting season for the Dbacks, who have won 80-plus games in four straight seasons but still have just their surprise 2023 World Series run to show for it.
11) Guardians (84-76): A
The Guardians did what they do this season. Prevent runs. Score just enough. Fly under the radar for most of the year. Then round into form late to (most likely) win another AL Central title.
12) White Sox (83-77): A
This could still become an A+ if the White Sox wind up winning the AL Central. But even if not, the South Siders have been the most pleasant surprise in the majors this season, going from three straight 100-loss seasons to an upstart playoff berth with their young and promising roster.
13/14) Astros/Rangers (79-81): Incomplete
To be clear, neither of these teams has had a good 2026. And yet, they both enter the final days of the season with a chance to win the AL West — even though they can finish no better than .500. It will be the first time in MLB history a team will make the playoffs without a winning record. What a year in the AL West.
15) Pirates (81-79): C+
Good news: The Pirates avoided a losing record for the first time since 2018. Bad news: It wasn’t enough to keep them in playoff contention despite a surprisingly productive year from their offense.
16) Marlins (79-81): C+
The Marlins flirted with playoff contention for a while before ultimately fading down the stretch. They could be poised to take another step next year. Then again, they’ve looked that way before (remember that surprise playoff appearance in 2023?) and been unable to keep progressing.
17) Orioles (79-82): D
The Orioles’ signing of Pete Alonso worked out. But little else did in Baltimore this year. The once-budding contender has now missed the playoffs in two straight years after being swept in back-to-back postseasons the two years before that.
18) Blue Jays (78-82): D
As if the Blue Jays’ post-pennant campaign wasn’t bad enough, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. provided one more low point with his comments about his $500 million contract this week. There is hope for next season. But this year stung.
19) Cardinals (77-83): B
Given nonexistent preseason expectations, the rebuilding Cardinals mostly accomplished what they wanted to this year. They have young talent in Jordan Walker and JJ Wetherholt. They have rebuilt what is now a highly ranked farm system. And they look like a team capable of making a jump in 2027 and beyond.
20) Nationals (76-84): C
The Nats were never serious playoff contenders (their MLB-record 42 blown saves made sure of that). But they have identified a core of young talent to build around. Whether they will spend to add the necessary pieces around them, however, remains to be seen.
21) Mets (73-87): D-
The Mets can only hope this train wreck of a year serves as some sort of cleanse as they look to retool their roster this winter. The only thing that saved this from being an F was their second-half performance under another interim-now-turned-permanent manager in Andy Green.
22) Twins (76-84): C
For some reason, the Twins were intent on being playoff contenders this year. For a while, they hung around in a bad AL wild-card race. But in the end, they’ve wound up back where they started: With an OK, but not-at-all contending, roster that leaves them stuck in MLB’s no-man’s land.
23) Tigers (75-85): D
How much will the Tigers rue their decision to not maximize Tarik Skubal’s trade value by dealing him last winter? It could depend, first and foremost, on River Ryan’s development in their rotation. At the least, he offered signs of promise with a scoreless three-inning debut with the team this week.
24) Reds (74-86): D
Whatever momentum the Reds thought they were building after last year’s postseason berth vanished this summer, despite Elly De La Cruz cementing himself as one of the best players in baseball. The next time their owner asks why they aren’t the Brewers, someone should hold up a mirror.
25) Mariners (74-86): F
At the beginning of the year, only the Dodgers had a higher probability of making the playoffs (according to FanGraphs’ computer models) than the Mariners’ 80.9% mark. Instead, they suffered what might be the most disappointing season in their long-tortured history. They could be good again next year. But this season was a reminder that’s anything but a guarantee.
26) Royals (68-92): D
Another disastrous Royals season leaves them facing an existential crisis, trying to figure out how to return to competitiveness before they waste the prime of Bobby Witt Jr.’s career.
27) Giants (65-95): F
The Giants thought they could be contenders this year. Instead, they now find themselves at a crossroads. They have little choice but to run it back with their thus-far disappointing core of Willy Adames, Matt Chapman and Rafael Devers (plus Logan Webb). But this year, they looked a long way off from even being competitive.
28) Athletics (64-96): D-
There was some thought before the year that the Athletics’ young roster could be feisty. Now, the only question is how much longer they have to waste away in their minor-league ballpark purgatory.
29) Angels (62-98): C
This grade has little to do with the Angels’ on-field product, as they flirt with what would be the first 100-loss season in franchise history, and everything to do with the changes they’ve made behind the scenes. New owner. New front office. And for the first time in a while, new reason for long-term hope.
30) Rockies (57-103): D
The best thing we can say about the Rockies: They proved slightly tougher to beat during this 100-loss season, as opposed to each of the three previous ones they have suffered the last three years. Progress!
Awards Predictions
NL MVP: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
AL MVP: Yordan Alvarez, Astros
NL Cy Young: Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers
AL Cy Young: Cam Schlittler, Yankees
NL Rookie of the Year: Sal Stewart, Reds
AL Rookie of the Year: Kevin McGonigle, Tigers
NL Reliever of the Year: Mason Miller, Padres
AL Reliever of the Year: Louis Varland, Blue Jays
