item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays, the New York Yankees, and the Boston Red Sox have all punched their ticket to the postseason. With the final week of the 2026 MLB regular season already upon us, several other American League squads are playing for a place in October, too.
Even the Rays and Yankees technically have to decide who wins the AL East, with the former enjoying a hefty advantage heading into the final week, needing just one win over the Bombers to secure it. After that, there are two wide-open divisions and an exciting competition for the last Wild Card spot.
Here’s where every team stands in the race:
Tampa Bay Rays
Remaining games: 4 @ Yankees, 3 @ Phillies
Current record: 95-60
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL East (6 games ahead of NYY)
Final week outlook: The Rays have been, far and away, the top team in the American League by win-loss record, and unless something really crazy happens, they will enter the postseason with a first-round bye and wait for the winner of the battle between the top two Wild Cards—the Yankees and Red Sox—in the Division Series. They’ll still try to play competitive games after clinching, as they certainly wouldn’t say no to having home-field advantage over NL teams in a potential World Series matchup* as they seek their first championship in franchise history, but the pressure this week is much lighter.
*We’re keeping the focus on the AL in this post, but for those curious, Tampa Bay’s 95-60 record currently trails the Dodgers’ 96-60 and the Brewers’ 98-58. Atlanta trails at 92-64. The Dodgers have the Padres and Giants to end 2026 while the Brewers have the Phillies and Cardinals, and the Braves have the Reds and Marlins.
New York Yankees
Remaining games: 4 vs. Rays, 3 vs. Orioles
Current record: 89-66
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 2nd in AL East (6 games behind TB); 1st in Wild Card race (5.5 games ahead of 2nd Wild Card spot, held by BOS)
Final week outlook: Unless they sweep the Rays and Orioles, the Yankees virtually have no chance of winning the AL East crown. Instead, they will likely enter the postseason as the top Wild Card team, as they have a healthy cushion over the Red Sox, their likely foe in the Wild Card round. The odds of that series being at Fenway rather than Yankee Stadium are extremely low, especially since New York has the tiebreaker over Boston.
Boston Red Sox
Remaining games: 3 vs. Guardians, 3 vs. Cubs
Current record: 84-72
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 3rd in AL East, 2nd in Wild Card race (5.5 games behind NYY for top WC spot, 4 games ahead of CHW, owners of the 3rd WC spot)
Final week outlook: The Red Sox are highly unlikely to move from the second AL Wild Card spot, since they have a four-game cushion over the White Sox, owners of the third slot, and are 5.5 games behind the Yanks for the top one. They’ve been all but locked into this spot for awhile now and just clinched their playoff berth yesterday with Houston’s loss to Atlanta.
Cleveland Guardians
Remaining games: 3 @ Red Sox, 3 @ Royals
Current record: 81-75
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL Central (1 game ahead of CHW)
Final week outlook: Eyeing their third consecutive division title and seventh since 2016, the Guardians are currently one game up in the race for the AL Central, but need to avoid a tie with the White Sox at the top because Chicago owns the tiebreaker. Cleveland is peaking at the right time, though, and José Ramírez is finally starting to show some signs of a breakthrough at the plate. If that’s the case, they will be dangerous with a strong young core and two aces at the top: AL strikeout leader Gavin Williams and Rookie of the Year contender Parker Messick. Second baseman Travis Bazzana isn’t too shabby of a rookie, either.
Chicago White Sox
Remaining games: 3 @ Royals, 3 vs. Rockies
Current record: 80-76
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 2nd in AL Central (1 game behind CLE), 3rd in Wild Card race (3 games ahead of HOU and TOR, 5 ahead of BAL)
Final week outlook: Chicago’s lack of quality starting pitching seems to have caught up to them in September, but they are still a dangerous team that is trending towards its first postseason appearance since 2021. They have a chance to win the AL Central: all they need to do is finish in at least a tie with the Guardians, and though both the Pale Hose and Guards will face the Royals this week, the Southsiders have an easier other foe in the Rockies. Remember, winning the division would likely even give Chicago the second seed in the AL and a first-round bye to face the victor of the AL West/last Wild Card matchup.
It’s already been an improbably great season for the White Sox, as merely getting a winning season would’ve been a huge success for a team that lost a modern record 121 games in 2024 and 102 last year. But missing out at this point would still be quite the disappointment.
Texas Rangers
Remaining games: 3 vs. Mets, 3 @ Twins
Current record: 78-78
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 1st in AL West (1 game ahead of HOU)
Final week outlook: If the Rangers finish with more wins than the Astros, they will capture the AL West despite their thoroughly mediocre record (the Mariners’ deeply disappointing 2026 really made the division a mess). It’s a key week in Texas, as the range of outcomes is wide: they could win the division and finish as high as the second seed if they can best the AL Central champ’s line; they could be the final Wild Card squad, or they could miss the playoffs entirely for the third year in a row since winning it all in 2023 behind two-time World Series MVP Corey Seager.
It’s important to note that the Rangers need to beat the Astros by at least one game to take the AL West crown because Houston owns the tiebreaker. The Rangers own tiebreakers against the Orioles, Guardians, and Blue Jays, and lost against the White Sox and, as explained, the Astros. The AL West winner is a near-lock to face the worst Wild Card team in the first round, though they will host the best-of-three.
Toronto Blue Jays
Remaining games: 3 @ Orioles, 3 vs. Reds
Current record: 77-79
Current position in division/Wild Card race: tied with HOU for 4th in Wild Card standings, 3 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: Last year’s AL champs can’t win their division: their only path to the playoffs is the third and final Wild Card spot. With that in mind, however, they would need to finish ahead of both the White Sox and the Rangers because both of them own the tiebreaker against Toronto. It sure doesn’t help that ace Dylan Cease was scratched from his next start and is undergoing an MRI.
The Jays tied the season series against Houston, which, in the event of a tie at the third WC spot between them, would take us to intra-divisional record to decide. There, Toronto is 25-24 against AL East opponents, and the Astros are 22-24 vs. AL West foes, presently giving the Jays the edge, though that could change this week since they both face intra-divisional rivals.
For what it’s worth, Toronto won the tiebreakers against the Guardians and the Orioles.
Houston Astros
Remaining games: 2 @ Mariners, 4 @ A’s
Current record: 77-79
Current position in division/Wild Card race: tied with TOR for 4th in Wild Card standings, 3 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: Much like the White Sox in the AL Central, the Astros are one game behind in their division and own the tiebreaker against the Rangers, so all they need to do is catch them by the end of the week. They have lost three straight, though, with a -59 run differential, so despite the best efforts of MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez, they aren’t particularly good. We have seen plenty of mediocre squads make it in the past, so they definitely have a chance — especially since they get to play the mostly-hapless M’s and A’s this week.
Houston can still qualify via the last Wild Card, but the division presents a smoother path. Since we’re running through them, they own tiebreakers vs. the White Sox, Guardians, and Rangers, losing vs. the Orioles and tying vs. Toronto.
Baltimore Orioles
Remaining games: 3 vs. Blue Jays, 3 @ Yankees
Current record: 75-81
Current position in division/Wild Card race: 6th in Wild Card standings, 5 games behind the 3rd spot (CHW)
Final week outlook: At this point, the Orioles need a miracle to get in. They needed to sweep the Brewers this past weekend to put themselves in a position to compete. Instead, they got swept themselves. Baltimore won tiebreakers against the White Sox and the Astros, and lost against the Rangers, Guardians, and Blue Jays. But again, they have essentially no shot whatsoever. That final weekend series in the Bronx could’ve been interesting; alas.

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell
item.description: The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series. "Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not
item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.title: [FanGraphs] Bobby Witt Jr. and the Off-Peak MVP Season
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
item.description: Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr
item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Astros' Yordan Alvarez Shares Rare Frustration over Brutal Series Against Braves
item.dc:creator: Maddy Dickens; Unknown
item.description: There was a point not so long ago that it felt like the Houston Astros were about to run away with the AL West and were actually fighting for the No.2 spot in the American League playoff rankings which would have led to a first-round bye. item.content:encoded:
There was a point not so long ago that it felt like the Houston Astros were about to run away with the AL West and were actually fighting for the No.2 spot in the American League playoff rankings which would have led to a first-round bye. Well, a lot can change in a week, especially in the AL.
Right now, there is a very mediocre turtle race going on in both the AL West and for the final wild card spot, but right now the Astros are seemingly taking themselves out of that race as they continue to lose games.
After being swept by the Atlanta Braves, at home no less, Houston is three games out of the last wild card slot and one behind the Texas Rangers for the division as they are now two games under the .500 line.
Not too long ago, the Astros had a three-game lead over the Rangers, but boy, have the wheels fallen off the rails as of late. Designated hitter Yordan Alvarez shared his rare public frustrations, via interpreter, with The Athletic's Chandler Rome (subscription required).
Alvarez called a team meeting after the loss on Sunday and called this weekend "three slaps in the face," per Rome. It is very rare that their veteran shows any sort of negative emotion out in the open, but who can blame him?
The Astros are now 4-10 since the first Saturday of September, and they, simply put, are not a postseason team. The ballclub has a day off to regroup before embarking on their final road trip of the season, and they are ultimately feeling October baseball slip through their fingers.
What Went Wrong Against the Braves This Weekend
The first two games of the Braves series never really felt like the Astros were in much control as Houston dropped the opener 6-2 as the Braves hit three home runs with neither the offense nor defense really firing on all cylinders.
However, the biggest heartbreaker was Sunday afternoon at Daikin Park as the Astros went 0-for-3 with the bases loaded, and it was 1-1 going into the sixth inning when Bryan King threw a meatball down the middle of the plate that turned into a three-run homer.
It is also impossible to ignore Cam Smith's struggles that have gone on well before the series with Atlanta, as he is now in a 0-for-25 drought while hitting sub.150 over his last 30 games, which doesn't complement a lackluster bullpen that is now without Steven Okert for the rest of the year.
This is a team game, so no individual player is responsible for the issues that Houston is facing, but time is rapidly running out for them to figure it out.
Maddy Dickens resides in Loveland, Colorado. She grew up with two older brothers, where their lives revolved around sports. She earned a master's degree in business management from Tarleton State University while simultaneously playing basketball and competing in rodeo at the collegiate level. She successfully parlayed a reserve national championship into a professional rodeo career and now stays involved in upper-level athletics by writing for On SI on several different MLB teams' pages, along with some NCAA sites.

item.content:encoded:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.
Will Schwarber or PCA lead the Majors in home runs?
Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.

item.content:encoded:
Yordan Álvarez edificó con los porcentajes un muro que parece impenetrable para merecerse el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana. En la semana final de la fase regular saca 34 puntos sobre Junior Caminero en promedio de bateo (.313-.277), uno de los renglones que encabeza detrás de la Triple Corona.
Pero donde se separa del resto por cuerpo entero es en la principal referencia ofensiva de hoy, el OPS. Es el único en toda la MLB que supera los 1.000 (1.027), 135 puntos sobre el .892 del de los Rays. La superioridad es apreciable en la frecuencia de embasarse (.430-.363) y de extrabases (.597-.515).
Ante esa respetable ventaja porcentual, que hace que en Las Vegas den como un hecho su MVP, clasifique Houston o no, los partidarios de Caminero argumentan el aporte defensivo que hace el dominicano al salir a diario al terreno.
En la ecuación que arroja el WAR de FanGraphs y Baseball-Reference, el ajuste posicional le da a Caminero +2.5 carreras como antesalista y Álvarez -17.5 como un bateador designado que no aporta con el guante.
Antes de salir al terreno, el quisqueyano sale delante, pero el de Las Tunas remonta con el madero hasta liderar en esa casilla.
Lo que dice la Sabermetría
Hay métricas que dejan bien parado a "La Máxima" como 3B, otras no. Baseball Info Solutions dice que ha salvado 4 carreras defensivas, un salto impresionante con relación a las -5 de 2025.
Sin embargo, Savant "opina" todo lo contrario. En OAA saca -12 out por encima del promedio, es decir, la cantidad de outs que hace con relación al antesalista average.
El cálculo se apoya en cámaras e inteligencia artificial que miden desde la velocidad de salida del batazo, el ángulo del roletazo, la distancia recorrida hacia la bola y la fuerza/precisión del disparo a la base.
En carreras prevenidas, medido por Statscat, queda con -9. Es líder en errores entre los defensores de la esquina caliente (19) en la Americana.
A pesar de que Álvarez, quien ha jugado 24 partidos en el prado izquierdo (con -5 DRS) y 129 como designado, queda con -1.7 WAR defensivos al sumar las 6.7 ofensivas totaliza 6.3, líder de todo el béisbol. Caminero, con 0.7 defensivas, tiene 5.7 en total.
De las 25.6 WAR de los jugadores de posición de los Rays, Caminero lidera el aporte con 5.7 (22.2 %). En cambio, Álvarez es responsable de 6.3 de las 19 de los Astros o el 33.1 %.
Dicho esto, el cubano ha sido más determinante para Houston que Caminero para Tampa, a pesar del abismo competitivo entre ese salvaje Este y el mediocre Oeste.

item.title: [UNANIMO Deportes] Nolan Arenado lidera remontada de Diamondbacks ante Yankees - UNANIMO Deportes
item.dc:creator: Juan David Perez
item.description: Los Arizona Diamondbacks volvieron a demostrar que saben reaccionar cuando están contra las cuerdas. Este domingo, una noche inspirada de Nolan Arenado, quien conectó su tercer grand slam de la temporada, fue clave para que Arizona remontara y derrotara 8-4 a los New York Yankees. - LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡José Ramírez llega a las 1,000 carreras impulsadas! - LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡Los Atlanta Braves aseguran su boleto a los playoffs! - LEER MÁS SOBRE: New York Yankees 9- 2 Diamondbacks: Resultados y crónica
item.content:encoded:
Los Arizona Diamondbacks volvieron a demostrar que saben reaccionar cuando están contra las cuerdas. Este domingo, una noche inspirada de Nolan Arenado, quien conectó su tercer grand slam de la temporada, fue clave para que Arizona remontara y derrotara 8-4 a los New York Yankees.
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡José Ramírez llega a las 1,000 carreras impulsadas!
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡Los Atlanta Braves aseguran su boleto a los playoffs!
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: New York Yankees 9- 2 Diamondbacks: Resultados y crónica
La jugada que terminó por cambiar el rumbo del encuentro llegó en la quinta entrada. Los Diamondbacks habían conseguido llenar las bases frente al abridor de Nueva York, Will Warren, quien dejó el montículo para darle paso al relevista Brent Headrick.
El pitcher logró retirar a Geraldo Perdomo con un ponche para conseguir el segundo out, pero después vino el descontrol. Headrick otorgó una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll, situación que permitió que Arizona sumara una carrera y dejara las bases listas para Arenado.
Con cuenta de 2-1, el tercera base no perdonó. Arenado encontró el lanzamiento y mandó la pelota por encima de la barda para completar el grand slam y darle la vuelta al partido. Fue el noveno cuadrangular con las bases llenas de su carrera, además de que alcanzó al cubano Yordan Álvarez, de los Houston Astros, como líder de las Grandes Ligas en grand slams durante esta temporada.
Pero el poder ofensivo de Arizona no se limitó a Arenado. Perdomo también tuvo una tarde productiva al conectar un sencillo productor en la primera entrada y posteriormente un triple que llevó otra carrera al plato durante el séptimo episodio.
Los Yankees, por su parte, habían respondido con fuerza en el tercer inning. Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones conectaron cuadrangulares consecutivos dentro de esa entrada frente al abridor de Arizona, Corbin Burnes, para mantener con vida a Nueva York.
Sin embargo, la ofensiva neoyorquina se apagó después de ese episodio. El bullpen de Arizona tomó el control y, encabezado por Justin Martínez, consiguió limitar a los Yankees a solamente tres imparables durante las últimas 6 entradas. Martínez se apuntó la victoria, la tercera de su temporada, con marca de 3-0.
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
Arenado héroe de Arizona
Con este triunfo, los Diamondbacks llegaron a 47 victorias conseguidas después de comenzar perdiendo, la cifra más alta de las Grandes Ligas. Arizona continúa además en la pelea con los Philadelphia Phillies por el último boleto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, aunque todavía se encuentra cuatro juegos por detrás cuando restan seis encuentros.
Del otro lado, los Yankees aún conservan posibilidades matemáticas de pelear por el Este de la Liga Americana, aunque necesitan cerrar la temporada con victorias y esperar resultados favorables. Nueva York comenzará el martes una serie de cuatro partidos ante los Tampa Bay Rays, actuales líderes divisionales, en territorio neoyorquino.
Por ahora, Arizona celebra una remontada más en una temporada en la que ha convertido los partidos complicados en una de sus principales características. Y esta vez, el golpe decisivo tuvo nombre y apellido: Nolan Arenado.

item.title: [MLB.com] Alvarez calls players' meeting to rally Astros after tough series vs. Braves
item.dc:creator: Brian McTaggart
item.description: HOUSTON -- The frustration oozed out of Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez with every word he spoke to reporters in a hushed clubhouse on Sunday afternoon. It was only moments before that the stoic Alvarez did something he hasn’t done much in his career, speaking up in a players’ meeting following a sweep at the hands of the Braves. “Basically for us, it was three slaps in the face they gave us right in front of our fans, especially,” Alvarez said through an interpreter. “Just use tomorrow to take it
item.content:encoded:
HOUSTON -- The frustration oozed out of Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez with every word he spoke to reporters in a hushed clubhouse on Sunday afternoon. It was only moments before that the stoic Alvarez did something he hasn’t done much in his career, speaking up in a players’ meeting following a sweep at the hands of the Braves.
“Basically for us, it was three slaps in the face they gave us right in front of our fans, especially,” Alvarez said through an interpreter. “Just use tomorrow to take it as a reset day and rest, and then the only thing left is to go out there and win the six games we have left.”
Six games on the road -- two against the Mariners in Seattle and four against the A’s in West Sacramento -- are the only games still guaranteed on the Astros’ schedule this season, but they’re hoping for more. Sunday afternoon’s 4-2 loss to the Braves at Daikin Park was Houston’s 10th in its past 14 games, dropping the Astros to 77-79.
“We have six chances to go out there and make the playoffs,” said Alvarez, who is chasing an American League MVP and Triple Crown entering the regular season’s final week.
“Listen, we’ve got to use tomorrow to really gather our thoughts and get a good plan together for the next week,” manager Joe Espada said. “No doubt about it that we need to bounce back and really dig deep and fight, because this series was not what we were expecting.”
Sunday’s script was reminiscent of Saturday’s 6-3 loss, when Braves slugger Ronald Acuna Jr. hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the seventh. The Astros’ led, 1-0, through five innings on Sunday before Bryan King allowed all four batters he faced to reach, capped by MIke Yastrzemski’s three-run homer in the sixth that made it 4-1.
The Astros went 0-for-3 with the bases loaded and did little to back starting pitcher Hunter Brown, who struck out 10 batters in five scoreless innings. Brown also walked three batters and was pulled after throwing 98 pitches, but Houston’s battered bullpen couldn’t hold the lead for the second game in a row.
“We can still make a big push here,” Brown said. “We’re right in it. We’re not dead yet. That’s what we’re going to do, give it our all these last six games and find out where we are after that.”
Alvarez refused to divulge what was said in his speech or who else spoke up, but outfielder Taylor Trammell said his message carried weight.
“He doesn’t talk much and when he speaks, there’s a presence,” Trammell said. “This was not a ‘hoorah’ or anything like that. It’s just like, ‘Hey guys, Easy. Just be easy with it,’ and hearing it from him, it means something. You see the way he’s played all year and you can’t tell me there hasn’t been any nicks or bangs for him. And he’s going out there every single day and being the best hitter in the game right now. That’s what he’s doing. And so when he says something and he talks, you listen.”
Veteran first baseman Christian Walker said Alvarez’s speech stressed a sense of urgency facing the Astros, who were knocked out of first place on Saturday for the first time since late July. Houston missed the postseason by one game last year, ending its run of eight consecutive playoff appearances.
Alvarez challenged his teammates to get back to October.
“Everybody is going to receive things differently, but younger guys who haven’t been to the postseason, it feels like there’s a lot of pressure right now, and there is,” Walker said. “And that’s a good thing, because we played ourselves into a spot to be competitive. I think any time a vet can address the team, especially somebody like Yordan, if nothing else, for everybody to feel the calmness he brings to the table. That can be helpful.”
The Mariners (73-83), whose slim playoff hopes are still alive, would love nothing more to spoil it for the Astros, who are 2-9 against Seattle. Houston ends the season playing in a Minor League ballpark in West Sacramento that can be about as unpredictable as it gets and wants to leave nothing to chance.
“These next two teams have nothing to lose,” Walker said. “Their goal is to knock us out. I’ve been on teams where we’ve been in that position before and it can be a dangerous spot. I think it’s a good reminder to come into these cities with a fire and a sense of urgency, and prepare to come in and win some baseball games.”

item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez Gives Bold Quote, Calls Team Meeting as Astros Fall in MLB Playoff Standings
Yordan Alvarez was not pleased after the Houston Astros were swept by the Atlanta Braves over the weekend, leaving them a game behind the Texas Rangers in the AL West with just six games remaining.
The superstar slugger told reporters he called a team meeting following Sunday's 4-2 loss:
Alvarez, 29, has more than done his part this season, hitting .313 with 40 homers, 99 RBI, 98 runs and a 1.027 OPS. He's likely going to be the AL MVP, though it likely won't mean nearly as much if the Astros—who have lost 10 of their last 14 games—fail to reach the postseason.
They will have two games remaining against the Seattle Mariners and four against the Athletics to salvage the season. The Rangers will finish with three games against the New York Mets and three games against the Minnesota Twins.

item.title: [MLB.com] These stars have turned their seasons around in the second half
item.dc:creator: Theo DeRosa
item.description: One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run. While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success. Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half. All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified. Hitters Alex Bregman, Cubs For as good as National League MVP Award
item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

item.content:encoded:
Conecta Isaac Paredes su jonrón número 22, pero los Astros pierden liderato de su división
El hermosillense esta a nueve cuandrangulares de su récord en Grandes Ligas
Isaac Paredes conectó este sábado su cuadrangular número 22 en la presente campaña de MLB, aunque no fue suficiente para evitar que los Astros de Houston cayeran por 6-3 ante los Bravos de Atlanta y cayeran al segundo lugar en la División Oeste de la Liga Americana.
El tablazo del hermosillense llegó en el cierre de la primera entrada, ante el abridor Grant Holmes, quien había dominado a Jeremy Peña y a Yordan Álvarez iniciando esa tanda.
Paredes remolcó una segunda anotación en la tercera baja, con un sencillo al jardín derecho que fue suficiente para impulsar a Peña después después que este último había conectado un triple.
El mexicano también anotó dos carreras, una vez que en el octavo episodio negoció una base por bolas y más tarde fue mandado al plato con doblete de Yainer Díaz.
Con siete campañas de experiencia en Grandes Ligas, la presente ya es la segunda mejor en términos de cuadrangulares para el sonorense, solo por detrás de los 31 conseguidos en 2023 con los Rays de Tampa Bay.
Ese jonrón también lo acercó a 10 del récord que ostenta Aurelio Rodríguez (124), el tercer jugador nacido en México con más cuadrangulares en Ligas Mayores. Vinicio Castilla (320) y Jorge Orta (130) encabezan la lista.
A los Astros de Houston les restan siete encuentros en la temporada regular, por lo que su marca podría incrementarse todavía más de aquí al próximo domingo 27 de septiembre.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yordan Alvarez Reaches 40 Home Runs and Keeps Triple Crown Pursuit Alive
item.dc:creator: Yirsandy Rodriguez; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Since he hit Seth Lugo’s fastball, Yordan Alvarez knew that ball was out of the park. The hit came off at 107.2 mph and landed 385 feet into right field, right in the second-level seats at Daikin Park to give Houston a 4-1 lead over the Kansas City Royals earlier this week.
Thus continued Alvarez's pursuit of the Triple Crown—the last one was won by Miguel Cabrera in 2012 with the Detroit Tigers in the American League—, hitting his 40th home run of the season to join a select club in the history of the Astros and players born in Cuba.
He became just the fifth player in Astros history to reach that mark:
• Jeff Bagwell — 47 (2000), 43 (1997), 42 (1999)
• Lance Berkman — 45 (2006), 42 (2002)
• Richard Hidalgo — 44 (2000)
• Alex Bregman — 41 (2019)
• Yordan Alvarez — 40 (2026)
The Hall of Fame member, Jeff Bagwell, was the first Houston hitter to hit 40 or more home runs in a season, when he achieved the feat with 43 home runs in 1997, at 29 years old. In his entire career, he finished recording three similar seasons (1997, 1999 and 2000).
The 47 home runs he hit in the 2000 season remained marked as the most in club history. Richard Hidalgo (44 HR in 2000) and Alex Bregman (41 in 2019) have been the youngest hitters to enter the club, both at 25 years old. But this season, he has made the difference in an unprecedented season for a 40-home-run hitter who has worn the Astros uniform, as he leads the league with an offensive line of .311/.429/.598, 1.027 OPS, 189 OPS+, 319 total bases, 103 walks and 32 intentional walks.
After going through a slump in his home run production, with only five in the last 40 games, Alvarez has heated up again with a pair of home runs in his last 10 at-bats, both in the series that Houston won 2-1 against the Royals. Now he is one home run away from tying Tampa Bay Rays third baseman Junior Caminero, who leads the American League with 41, and three RBIs away from reaching Pete Alonso (102).
Houston has eight games remaining to finish the regular season, two more against the Atlanta Braves at home, a two-game road trip against the Seattle Mariners and four against the Athletics.
Another Chapter of Glory Among Cuban Hitters
Alvarez also joined the list of only four Cuban-born hitters who have hit at least 40 home runs in the Majors. The legendary Cooperstown Hall of Fame member, Tony Pérez, was the first Cuban-born hitter to hit at least 40 home runs in a season, when he reached the milestone in the 1970 season with the Cincinnati Reds’ “Big Red Machine.”
Eighteen years later, José Canseco appears on the historical list, at just 23 years old, in his historic 40-40 season (42 home runs and 40 stolen bases), wearing the Oakland Athletics uniform in 1988.
Canseco entered the club four times, repeating the feat with 41 home runs in 1991 and 46 in 1998. Another who reached the milestone was Rafael Palmeiro, who leads the group of Cuban hitters with four 40-home-run seasons (1998-1999 and 2000 and 2002). Seventeen years later, Jorge Soler hit 48 home runs with the Royals and took ownership of the record for Cubans in a single season, leaving behind Palmeiro’s 47-home-run seasons in 1999 and 2001.
For the first time in the club, Alvarez can go much farther if he manages to regain his home run pace in these last nine games. Before reaching the August and September stretch, his worst month in production had been June when he hit six home runs in 26 games. However, as we saw before, he has been able to take only five balls out of the park since August 1 until now, and that has made the race against Caminero become much more attractive.
Alvarez still has the possibility of reaching a Triple Crown by leading all three offensive categories in all of MLB, a feat that no hitter has accomplished since Mickey Mantle with the New York Yankees in 1956 (.353 BA, 52 HR, 130 RBI).
Yirsandy is a baseball writer specializing in MLB coverage with experience across multiple teams and storylines. He currently writes for Diamond Centric, where he covers the New York Mets, San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, and Kansas City Royals. My work focuses on game coverage, player analysis, and storytelling that connects performance with context. My Substack has also been an important part of my writing development, where I’ve built much of my baseball coverage and storytelling voice over time. I’m passionate about combining reporting, research, and thoughtful analysis to produce engaging baseball content for readers.
